narrative:
The model predicted a 96% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this risk, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year class rank was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward not passing. Your LSAT score was the third biggest contributor and similarly increased the likelihood of failure.

In each case these features worked against you because your performance sat well below the typical level seen among students who were admitted. Your first-year ranking placed you in the second decile compared with an average of sixth decile for accepted students. By year three you had fallen to the bottom decile, while admitted students averaged around the sixth. Your LSAT of 28 was also noticeably lower than the 37-point average among those who received offers.

Your undergraduate GPA, family income, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the overall picture.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach a score closer to the mid-30s or higher. Stronger results in these areas would significantly lower the model’s estimated risk of bar exam failure and make future applications far more competitive. (248 words)
